notes:
Task and constraints: Return the longest word that can be built one character at a time from other words in the list, breaking ties lexicographically.
Idea: Build a trie of all words, then traverse it only through prefixes represented by trie nodes.
Technique and why it applies: Each complete word stores its input index under '$'. Traversal updates the best answer when it reaches a terminal node and pushes only child nodes of the current prefix.
Invariant: The traversal stack contains trie nodes reachable through prefixes already visited; valid extensions are explored from each terminal prefix.
Edge cases: The code references defaultdict without importing it. Starting with list(root.values()) traverses first-letter nodes, and the problem's prefix requirement means nodes should only be expanded from a valid terminal word; as written it pushes children even when the current node is not terminal.
Complexity: Trie construction is O(total characters) and traversal visits trie nodes, with O(total characters) space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Merge accounts that share any email address, returning each merged account's emails sorted.
Idea: Repeatedly merge accounts with the same name and overlapping email sets until no further changes occur.
Technique and why it applies: The code unions email sets for same-name accounts and tracks indices it has merged. Repeating the entire merge pass is intended to combine transitive overlaps across multiple accounts.
Invariant: Each pass attempts to merge directly overlapping same-name accounts; the outer loop continues until the result stabilizes.
Edge cases: Matching names alone do not prove accounts belong together; shared email is the actual relation, but the code merges same-name accounts even without overlap in some cases. It can also fail to mark the current index in ls and uses sets that lose ordering until a later sort.
Complexity: Repeated passes and set operations can be quadratic or worse in the number of accounts and emails, with O(total emails) storage. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Merge accounts belonging to the same person when they share an email address.
Idea: Assign each distinct email an ID and union all emails appearing in the same account.
Technique and why it applies: Union-find connects the first email in each account to every other email. After processing all accounts, emails are grouped by representative, sorted, and prefixed with their stored name.
Invariant: Every email in one connected component belongs to the same merged account.
Edge cases: Accounts are assumed to contain at least one email; otherwise account[1] fails. Union-find chooses roots by numeric order rather than rank, but path compression still helps. If one email appears under inconsistent names, the last assigned mapping is not updated because only new emails receive names.
Complexity: Processing is near O(E α(E)) for E email occurrences, plus sorting each merged group; storage is O(E). No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Remove line and block comments from source code, joining lines that are connected by a block comment.
Idea: Scan characters while tracking whether the parser is inside a block comment; discard // suffixes and /*...*/ regions.
Technique and why it applies: Outside a block, ordinary characters append to new_str. Inside a block, scanning continues until */; a line is emitted only when accumulated content is nonempty and the block has ended.
Invariant: inComment indicates whether characters should be ignored across line boundaries, and new_str holds current uncommented text.
Edge cases: The code preserves accumulated text across lines inside block comments. It does not append empty output lines, as required. A line comment is recognized only when two characters remain, correctly handling the final character.
Complexity: Every source character is scanned once, giving O(total characters) time and O(total output) space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Remove // line comments and /*...*/ block comments from a list of source lines.
Idea: Maintain a block-comment flag and a buffer for text that remains after removing comments.
Technique and why it applies: Opening and closing markers toggle in_block; line comments break scanning outside blocks. newline collects characters across source lines until the block closes, allowing fragments around a block comment to join.
Invariant: newline contains the uncommented portion of the current logical output line, potentially accumulated across multiple source lines.
Edge cases: A nonempty newline buffer is emitted only when not inside a block comment. Empty results are omitted. The parser correctly ignores comment markers while already inside a block.
Complexity: The scan is O(total source characters) and output buffer space is O(total retained characters). No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Find an index where the sum of values to its left equals the sum of values to its right.
Idea: Start with the total as right sum, subtract the current value as the scan advances, and track the left sum.
Technique and why it applies: After subtracting nums[i], right represents values strictly to the right of i. The code compares it to left before the next iteration.
Invariant: At index i, right is intended to exclude nums[i], while left should contain values before i.
Edge cases: The implementation updates left using nums[i-1] after subtracting nums[i], which double-counts the previous value across iterations and makes the left sum incorrect. It should compare before adding the current value to left.
Complexity: The method is O(n) time and O(1) space, but the update order makes the result incorrect for many inputs. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Return the pivot index where left and right sums are equal, or -1 if none exists.
Idea: Compute the total sum once, then maintain the sum of values strictly to the left of each index.
Technique and why it applies: At index i, the right sum is total-left_sum-num. Equality identifies the pivot; if not equal, num is added to left_sum before advancing.
Invariant: left_sum equals the sum of nums before the current index.
Edge cases: Empty input returns -1. Negative values are supported because the method relies only on addition and equality.
Complexity: One sum pass and one scan give O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space, matching author labels.

Task and constraints: Parse a chemical formula with element symbols, numeric counts, and nested parentheses, returning atom counts in sorted order.
Idea: Use a stack of dictionaries, one per parenthesized group, and accumulate element counts as tokens are scanned.
Technique and why it applies: Uppercase letters begin element names; digits multiply the preceding element or closing group. Closing a parenthesis pops its dictionary and adds multiplied counts to the parent.
Invariant: Each stack dictionary holds atom counts accumulated within one nesting level.
Edge cases: Elements without explicit numbers contribute one. The condition after an element checks lowercase characters awkwardly but element names are consumed in one run. Formula is assumed valid and nonempty.
Complexity: Each character is processed a constant number of times, with dictionary work over distinct elements; time is O(n) expected and space O(n). No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Return atom counts for a nested chemical formula in canonical sorted format.
Idea: Use a regular expression to tokenize element names, opening parentheses, closing parentheses, and their multipliers, then process tokens with a Counter stack.
Technique and why it applies: Element tokens add their count to the current Counter. Opening parentheses push a new Counter; closing parentheses multiply that group's counts and merge them into the parent.
Invariant: stk[-1] holds atom counts for the current nesting level, and each closing parenthesis merges a completed subformula upward.
Edge cases: A missing numeric multiplier defaults to one. The regex assumes a valid formula and ignores text that does not match a token; valid-input constraints are important.
Complexity: Tokenization and merging are O(n) expected time, with O(n) space for the token list and counters. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Return all integers in [left,right] divisible by each of their nonzero decimal digits.
Idea: Convert each candidate to a string, skip numbers containing zero, and test divisibility by every digit.
Technique and why it applies: A zero digit would cause division by zero and therefore disqualifies the number. For remaining digits, all(num % digit == 0) verifies the defining property.
Invariant: res contains exactly the candidates checked so far that pass every digit test.
Edge cases: Zero digits are explicitly skipped. The input range is positive, so negative-number string signs do not occur.
Complexity: For R candidates with at most d digits, time is O(Rd) and output space is O(R). No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: List self-dividing numbers between left and right inclusive.
Idea: Filter each candidate by checking that every decimal digit is nonzero and divides the number evenly.
Technique and why it applies: The generator iterates over the decimal string and rejects a number if any digit is zero or has a nonzero remainder. Only candidates passing all digit tests are returned.
Invariant: Each output number has passed the divisibility test for every digit in its decimal representation.
Edge cases: A digit zero causes immediate rejection through the lambda predicate. itertools is imported but unused.
Complexity: For R candidates and up to d digits per candidate, time is O(Rd) and output storage is O(R). No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Return numbers that are divisible by each digit they contain, with no zero digit.
Idea: Test each candidate by repeatedly extracting its last decimal digit with divmod.
Technique and why it applies: The remainder r is the current digit; zero or a non-divisor rejects the number. The quotient advances to the remaining leading digits until all digits pass.
Invariant: isDividingNumber returns True only after every digit of the original number has been tested.
Edge cases: Zero digits are rejected before modulo by zero can occur. The positive range ensures the loop terminates when n reaches zero.
Complexity: Each number requires O(log r) digit operations, so total time is O(R log r) and auxiliary space is O(log r) for integer processing, conventionally O(1) for fixed-width values. Author labels use the latter convention.

Task and constraints: Count distinct nonempty palindromic subsequences in a string over the alphabet a through d, modulo 10^9+7.
Idea: Memoize an interval recursion and, for each possible outer character, use its first and last occurrence in the interval.
Technique and why it applies: A distinct palindrome can be formed by wrapping any palindromic subsequence between matching copies of a chosen character; if only one occurrence exists, it contributes one. The recursion sums contributions for each alphabet character.
Invariant: memo[(start,end)] stores the number of distinct palindromic subsequences in that substring.
Edge cases: Empty intervals return zero. The fixed loop over 'abcd' relies on the problem's alphabet constraint; other characters would be ignored. Repeated occurrences are handled through first/last positions.
Complexity: There are O(n²) interval states and each scans the fixed four-character alphabet, giving O(n²) time and space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Recolor the connected four-direction region containing (sr,sc) with the requested color.
Idea: Use a queue-like collection to explore neighbors matching the original target color, recoloring each visited cell.
Technique and why it applies: Starting at the source, each matching neighbor is queued; recoloring marks it as processed so it no longer matches targetColor. The four direction arrays enumerate orthogonal neighbors.
Invariant: Every queued cell belongs to the original connected component, and recolored cells will not be enqueued again.
Edge cases: If new color equals target color, the method returns immediately. deque is referenced but not imported. The code uses pop(), so the traversal is actually depth-first rather than breadth-first; either is valid for flood fill.
Complexity: Each cell is processed at most once, giving O(mn) time and O(mn) worst-case queue/stack space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Fill the four-connected region of the starting pixel with newColor.
Idea: Recursively traverse neighboring cells that still have the starting cell's original color.
Technique and why it applies: The DFS checks bounds and color before modifying a cell. Marking the cell immediately prevents revisiting it, then the four direction offsets explore the connected component.
Invariant: Every cell changed to newColor has been reached from the starting cell through same-colored neighbors.
Edge cases: If the old color already equals newColor, the method returns without recursion, preventing infinite revisits. The code assumes a nonempty rectangular image and valid start coordinates.
Complexity: Each cell is visited once, giving O(mn) time and O(mn) worst-case recursion space. The author labels omit explicit space but time is correct.

Task and constraints: Simulate collisions among asteroids moving in a line, where positive move right and negative move left.
Idea: Maintain a stack of surviving asteroids and resolve collisions whenever a right-moving top meets a left-moving current asteroid.
Technique and why it applies: If the top is smaller in magnitude, it is popped and the same incoming asteroid continues colliding. Equal magnitudes destroy both; a larger top destroys the incoming asteroid.
Invariant: stack contains asteroids that have survived all collisions with previously processed asteroids.
Edge cases: Asteroids moving in the same direction never collide. The loop's else appends the incoming asteroid only when no break occurs, matching the intended collision outcome.
Complexity: Each asteroid is pushed once and popped at most once, so time is O(n) and space O(n). No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Return the asteroid states after all collisions, preserving surviving order.
Idea: Use a stack and resolve only the collision case where the stack top moves right and the incoming asteroid moves left.
Technique and why it applies: A smaller positive asteroid is popped and the same incoming asteroid is compared again. Equal magnitudes remove both; a larger positive asteroid remains and destroys the incoming one.
Invariant: result stores the surviving prefix after processing each asteroid.
Edge cases: Same-direction asteroids do not collide. The while-else structure appends x only if no collision branch breaks the loop.
Complexity: Every asteroid is appended at most once and popped at most once, giving O(n) time and O(n) space, matching author labels.

Task and constraints: Simulate all asteroid collisions and return the remaining asteroids in order.
Idea: Append positive asteroids directly; for negative asteroids, pop smaller positive asteroids until the collision is resolved.
Technique and why it applies: A left-moving asteroid only collides with a positive stack top. Smaller positives are removed; an equal top is also removed and the incoming asteroid is destroyed; if a larger positive remains, the incoming asteroid is discarded.
Invariant: result contains the collision-resolved survivors from the processed input prefix.
Edge cases: Negative asteroids with no positive top are appended. Equal magnitudes destroy both. The method relies on the stack order to ensure only adjacent approaching asteroids are compared.
Complexity: Each asteroid is pushed and popped at most once, so O(n) time and O(n) space, matching author labels.

Task and constraints: Evaluate a nested Lisp-like expression using add, mult, and let with scoped variable bindings.
Idea: Tokenize expression text incrementally and use a stack of prior token lists and environment copies for nested expressions.
Technique and why it applies: add and mult evaluate two operands through lookup; let processes variable/value pairs before returning the final expression. On entering a parenthesis, the current environment is copied, and on close the inner value is appended to the parent token.
Invariant: lookup represents the current lexical environment, while stk stores the parent parsing context and environment snapshot for each open expression.
Edge cases: Variable scopes must be restored after closing nested expressions. The code's evaluate for let mutates lookup, and copying the dictionary on every nesting level preserves outer bindings.
Complexity: Repeated environment copies and token concatenation can lead to O(n²) time and O(n²) space in the expression length, consistent with author labels.

Task and constraints: Find the largest integer no greater than n whose digits are non-decreasing from left to right.
Idea: Scan digits from left to right, and at the first descent decrement the preceding digit and replace the suffix with nines.
Technique and why it applies: Once digit i exceeds digit i+1, the current number violates monotonicity. Decrementing the left digit makes it no larger than the next digit; setting all later digits to nine maximizes the resulting suffix. The while loop backs up across equal digits to avoid creating a new descent.
Invariant: Before the first violation, the prefix is non-decreasing; the returned prefix-plus-nines is the largest valid number below the original prefix violation.
Edge cases: Already monotone input returns n unchanged. The backward loop handles runs of equal digits before the violation, such as 332.
Complexity: The digit scan and possible backward adjustment are O(d) time and O(d) space for d digits. No labels were supplied.
